summary:
Jujuy stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action binding on Jujuy as on every province. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. The same government dismissed transgender people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota and abolished INADI, the federal agency that handled discrimination complaints. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high nationally in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a ten-year record and a 62% increase on the previous year, averaging one every 38 hours. Security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space were the most frequently identified perpetrators, beatings the main modality, institutional violence up from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32% of 2025 incidents taking place in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators strangers to their victims. Jujuy sits under that national picture, and the sources record no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate figures for the province.

Activists report that police violence, already common against trans and travesti sex workers, has worsened and is worst outside the capital. An April 2025 report datelined Buenos Aires names Jujuy among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is even more severe, and describes the community's position as chaotic and desperate.
tangentialFactors:
Agencia Presentes published the national hate-crime figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. Trans organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins told the Washington Blade on 4 April 2025 that the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration even though marriage equality and anti-discrimination statutes remain in force.

Nationally recorded hate crime is concentrated in the largest urban centres, while activists place the sharpest deterioration in police conduct in the interior, which is where Jujuy is situated.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jujuy who were employed in the public sector under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed by the national government, and the abolition of INADI removed the federal body through which residents could bring discrimination complaints.

Transgender residents held in custody in the province fall under the second 2025 decree, which governs the housing of transgender people in prison. That matters because 32% of the hate crimes recorded nationally in 2025 occurred inside police stations or prisons, and institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025.

Anti-discrimination protection for residents rests on a combination of national and provincial laws rather than on a single federal agency. Jujuy has no local reporting body producing separate crime records, so incidents involving residents are counted only in national totals.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation brought against the 5 February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is not recorded in the sources available here; legal experts called the decree illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene, but no ruling is documented.

No Jujuy-specific hate-crime or police-violence figures exist in the inventory, and the national totals for 2025 are not disaggregated by province, so the severity of conditions in Jujuy rests on activists' testimony rather than on local statistics.

The sources do not identify Jujuy's own provincial anti-discrimination instrument by name, nor record whether the province's authorities have applied the two 2025 federal decrees locally, how the prison-housing decree is implemented in Jujuy's detention facilities, or whether any provincial remedy remains after the abolition of INADI. These points are unresolved on the available record.
